action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.rationale: Self-reported or bedside smell loss is not an MDS supportive criterion; olfactory loss on a validated test for age and sex is, and with no red flag it turns clinically probable into clinically established PD [Postuma_2015]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not diagnose vascular parkinsonism on the white matter hyperintensities alone in an asymmetric, upper-limb predominant parkinsonism with rest tremor
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) at 77: high risk of confusion, urinary retention and cognitive worsening
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable PD (MDS 2015): bradykinesia with left-hand rest tremor and rigidity, no absolute exclusion, no red flag; olfactory loss on a validated test (UPSIT 20/40, severe microsmia, when tested) is a second supportive criterion and makes it clinically established, otherwise the response to levodopa may add one [Postuma_2015]

Attribute the Fazekas 2 white matter change to coexisting small-vessel disease, not to the cause of the parkinsonism: the syndrome is asymmetric and upper-limb predominant with rest tremor, without stepwise course or lacunes in the basal ganglia, and the DaTscan shows an asymmetric presynaptic deficit [Marshall_2009]

Start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), and review the response after 2 to 3 months, measuring lying and standing blood pressure at each step because amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide add to orthostatic falls [NICE_NG71]
Continue secondary vascular prevention for the prior TIA and small-vessel disease: antiplatelet, statin, and blood pressure and glycaemic control

Refer for physiotherapy for gait, turning and balance with a regular exercise programme, and advise bedroom safety for the dream enactment (pad the bedside, remove sharp objects); prefer melatonin over clonazepam if treatment is needed, because clonazepam adds sedation and fall risk at 77

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic confusion: EEG does not separate PD from vascular parkinsonism
No inflammatory, infectious or rapidly progressive feature and no NPH picture on MRI: CSF has no role in this parkinsonism
No murmur, heart failure or new cardioembolic event; the TIA was 6 years ago: an echocardiogram does not inform the parkinsonism
No palpitations, syncope or new ischemic event: rhythm monitoring does not inform the parkinsonism
No dementia and MoCA 26/30: amyloid PET does not inform the PD versus vascular parkinsonism question, which the DaTscan addresses
No cardiac symptom, syncope or QT-prolonging drug planned: an ECG does not inform the parkinsonism
Formal autonomic testing is not part of the PD work-up; bedside orthostatic measurement suffices

differential.key_features: Coexisting small-vessel disease (Fazekas 2, prior TIA, hypertension, diabetes), not the cause of the parkinsonism: asymmetric upper-limb onset with rest tremor, insidious rather than stepwise course, preserved lower-limb gait, no basal ganglia lacunes, and an asymmetric presynaptic deficit on DaTscan
No dopamine receptor antagonist or other causative drug on the medication list; abnormal DaTscan
Evans index 0.29 and callosal angle 112 degrees with ventricles proportionate to sulci; upper-limb predominant syndrome; no urinary incontinence
No orthostatic symptoms, urinary incontinence or cerebellar signs; rest tremor; normal putamina and pons on MRI
Full vertical saccades and range, no falls, no eyelid-opening apraxia, normal midbrain on MRI
Pill-rolling rest tremor with re-emergence, bradykinesia with decrement and rigidity are not features of ET; no family history of tremor

key_clinical_evidence: Left-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, cogwheel rigidity and a 4-5 Hz pill-rolling rest tremor of the left hand that re-emerges at rest after voluntary suppression: parkinsonism with one supportive criterion (rest tremor) and no red flag [Postuma_2015]

Smell loss found only on informal bedside testing is not a supportive criterion; a validated test (UPSIT 20/40, severe microsmia) makes it one and the diagnosis clinically established, otherwise clinically probable PD until the levodopa response is known [Postuma_2015]

Reduced sense of smell and constipation for about 3 years, preceding the 2-year motor history, and witnessed dream enactment for 18 months: prodromal synucleinopathy markers that small-vessel disease does not cause [Berg_2015]
MRI: Fazekas 2 white matter change without basal ganglia, thalamic or capsular lacunes, normal ventricles, midbrain, pons and putamina, and absent right nigrosome-1 on SWI [Schwarz_2014]

DaTscan with reduced putaminal binding, right 0.88 and left 1.42 (normal >1.50), opposite the worse left side with caudate sparing: a presynaptic deficit, which pure vascular parkinsonism does not usually produce [Marshall_2009]
Insidious asymmetric upper-limb onset with preserved lower-limb gait and no stepwise course argues against vascular parkinsonism, which is typically lower-body predominant and symmetric [Tolosa_2021]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Vascular risk factors and the Fazekas 2 white matter change on MRI raise vascular parkinsonism, but the asymmetric upper-limb parkinsonism with rest tremor, the insidious course and the asymmetric presynaptic deficit on DaTscan point to PD; the white matter change is coexisting small-vessel disease

interactions: Amlodipine lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.

Hydrochlorothiazide lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall, more so with volume depletion; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
warnings: Amantadine is renally cleared: reduce the dose when creatinine clearance falls below 50 mL/min, and recheck renal function before and during use.
Metformin, sitagliptin, rosuvastatin, aspirin, calcium carbonate, cholecalciferol and docusate: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.
High-protein meals can reduce levodopa absorption; distribute protein evenly through the day.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. Dorothea Williams is a 77-year-old left-handed retired librarian who presents to the neurology clinic accompanied by her adult daughter for evaluation of progressive left arm stiffness and tremor. Her daughter first noticed a subtle resting tremor in her mother's left hand approximately two years ago while watching television together; the tremor would appear when her mother's hands were at rest and partially subside when she reached for an object. Over the past 18 months, Mrs. Williams has noticed increasing stiffness in her left arm and shoulder, which she initially attributed to arthritis. She reports that daily tasks requiring fine motor dexterity, such as handling coins, buttoning garments and writing, have become notably harder with her dominant left hand. Her handwriting has become progressively smaller and harder to read, requiring her to use large-print labels at the library before she retired. She notes that her left arm does not swing naturally when she walks and that turning requires several steps rather than one smooth pivot. She denies any prior significant falls, though she has felt unsteady twice when turning quickly and has self-limited her walking routes as a result.

Mrs. Williams has several well-established cardiovascular risk factors: hypertension for over two decades, type 2 diabetes mellitus for 14 years, and a transient ischemic attack six years ago. Her primary care physician, noting these risk factors alongside her gait changes, raised the possibility of vascular parkinsonism and referred her to neurology. The patient herself is concerned about whether she has had 'small strokes' causing her current difficulties. However, she and her daughter both emphasize that her arm symptoms started asymmetrically on the left, not with any step-wise deterioration or fall episode, and that the tremor is most prominent at rest rather than when walking. She endorses a reduced sense of smell that her daughter first noticed three years ago when Mrs. Williams failed to detect the aroma of food cooking. She also reports longstanding constipation managed with a daily stool softener for approximately three years. Her daughter, who stays overnight from time to time, has witnessed episodes of shouting and arm-swinging during sleep over the past 18 months, most recently during a stay last month; Mrs. Williams sometimes recalls a vivid dream of being chased. She notes no significant cognitive complaints. She denies visual hallucinations, urinary incontinence, or orthostatic lightheadedness. She has not been started on any dopaminergic medications to date. Her medication list is reviewed and no dopamine receptor antagonists are identified.

neurological_exam.additional: Olfaction subjectively reduced: cannot identify coffee or cinnamon odors on informal bedside testing. Seborrheic dermatitis of the nasolabial folds. No urinary incontinence.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact without dysmetria bilaterally. Heel-to-shin intact. Rapid alternating movements impaired in left hand (bradykinesia), right hand mildly slow. No intention tremor. No cerebellar ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements full in all directions without nystagmus. No vertical gaze palsy or saccadic slowing on vertical gaze. Horizontal saccades mildly hypometric bilaterally, greater on the right. Smooth pursuit mildly impaired. Facial expression mildly reduced, blinking rate decreased. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. No eyelid-opening apraxia.
neurological_exam.gait: Mild stooped posture. Gait initiation mildly hesitant. Reduced left arm swing with mild en bloc turning requiring 4-5 steps. Stride length mildly shortened bilaterally, left more than right. Upper-body predominance of motor slowing; lower extremity gait is reasonably preserved for age without freezing or prominent lower-limb shuffling. Romberg negative. Pull test: one to two retropulsive steps, self-corrects without falling.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 26/30: lost 1 point on delayed recall, 1 point on phonemic fluency, 1 point on serial sevens, 1 point on abstraction. Speech is mildly hypophonic but fluent, with intact comprehension, repetition, and naming. No aphasia, neglect, or apraxia. Affect mildly hypomimic.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal. Left upper extremity: mild cogwheel rigidity at the wrist and elbow, best appreciated with reinforcement. Right upper extremity: tone normal. Left lower extremity: tone mildly increased at the ankle. Right lower extremity: tone normal. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. Bradykinesia in the left hand with slow, decremental finger-tapping and reduced amplitude on rapid alternating movements; right hand finger-tapping mildly slow but with preserved amplitude. Resting tremor present in the left hand at 4-5 Hz, pill-rolling character, re-emerging at rest after voluntary suppression, accentuated by mental arithmetic. No tremor in the right hand, chin, or lower extremities. Progressive left-hand micrographia on handwriting sample.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. Glabellar reflex positive (fails to habituate after 5 taps).
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration mildly reduced at bilateral great toes, consistent with age and diabetes. Proprioception intact at toes bilaterally. No cortical sensory deficits.
